body:
What is reflection of sound?

When a sound wave encounters a suitable surface or obstacle, part of its energy may return into the original medium. This phenomenon is called the reflection of sound.

Reflection can occur at surfaces such as walls, cliffs, buildings and the boundaries between different materials.

For clear reflection, an obstacle should generally be sufficiently large compared with the sound's wavelength. A surface need not be perfectly smooth or polished to reflect sound.

Laws of reflection of sound

Sound follows the same geometrical laws of reflection as light.

  • The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection, with both measured from the normal to the reflecting surface.
  • The incident sound direction, reflected sound direction and normal at the point of incidence lie in the same plane.

The normal is an imaginary line perpendicular to the reflecting surface at the point where the sound strikes it.

These laws describe the directions of the incident and reflected sound waves.

Formation of an echo

An echo is a reflected sound heard separately from the original sound after a sufficient time delay.

For example, a person shouting near a distant cliff may hear the shout again after the sound travels to the cliff, reflects and returns.

The sensation of hearing persists for approximately 0.1 second. Therefore, a distinct echo normally requires a delay of at least about 0.1 second between the original sound and the returning sound.

Minimum distance required for a distinct echo

Suppose the speed of sound is 344 m/s and the minimum distinguishable delay is 0.1 s.

In this interval, sound travels:

\(344 \times 0.1 = 34.4\,\mathrm{m}\)

This is the total distance to the reflecting surface and back. Hence, when the source and listener are close together:

\(d = \frac{34.4}{2} = 17.2\,\mathrm{m}\)

Thus, under these conditions, the reflecting surface should be approximately 17.2 m or more from the source to produce a distinct echo.

This is not an absolutely fixed distance. It changes with sound speed, temperature, the relative positions of source and listener, and the audibility of the reflected sound.

Calculating distance using an echo

If a sound pulse travels to a reflecting surface and returns in time t, the distance d of that surface from the source is:

\(d = \frac{vt}{2}\)

Here, v is the speed of sound and t is the total time between producing the sound and receiving its echo.

Distance of a reflecting cliff

A person hears an echo 1 second after producing a sound. If the speed of sound is 344 m/s:

\(d = \frac{344 \times 1}{2} = 172\,\mathrm{m}\)

The cliff is 172 m away, assuming the source and listener are at approximately the same location.

Multiple echoes

A single sound can produce more than 1 echo when reflected from different distant surfaces. The returning sounds may arrive at different times because they have travelled different distances.

Successive reflections help explain some of the prolonged rolling character of thunder.

Prelims focus

  • Reflection of sound obeys the same laws of reflection as light.
  • The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
  • A distinct echo generally requires a delay of at least 0.1 s.
  • At 344 m/s, the minimum source-to-reflector distance is approximately 17.2 m under standard textbook assumptions.
  • Echo distance is calculated using \(d = vt/2\).
  • Trap: The echo time represents a round trip, not the one-way journey to the reflector.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 12, Sound, sections 12.3–12.3.1, printed pages 167–168; GCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 11, Sound, sections 11.3–11.3.1.]

pictures.caption: A sound reflected from a distant rocky surface may return as a distinct echo.

pictures.alt: Sound travels 17.2 m to a cliff and 17.2 m back in 0.1 s; divide the total 34.4 m by 2 to find the cliff distance.

title: Reflection of Sound and Formation of Echoes

body:
What is reverberation?

When sound is produced inside a large enclosed space, it may undergo repeated reflection from the walls, ceiling, floor and other surfaces.

These reflected sounds can overlap and cause the original sound to persist for some time, even after the source has stopped producing it.

This persistence of sound due to repeated reflections is called reverberation.

Reverberation: The continued presence of sound caused by repeated reflections within an enclosed space.

Difference between echo and reverberation

Echo and reverberation both arise from reflection, but they are not identical.

FeatureEchoReverberation
NatureDistinct repetition of a soundPersistence of sound
ReflectionsOne or more sufficiently delayed reflectionsMany overlapping reflections
PerceptionOriginal and reflected sounds can be distinguishedReflections merge with the original sound
Common exampleShout heard again near a distant cliffLingering sound in a large hall

A reflected sound does not automatically become a distinct echo. If reflected sounds return too quickly to be separately distinguished, they may contribute to the overall persistence or character of the sound instead.

Why excessive reverberation is undesirable

In an auditorium, classroom or conference hall, excessive reverberation can reduce the clarity of speech.

When one word continues to be heard through repeated reflections while the next word is spoken, the sounds overlap and become difficult to distinguish.

Some reflected sound can help distribute sound across a hall, but excessive or prolonged reflections interfere with clear hearing.

Reducing reverberation

Reverberation is controlled by reducing the amount of sound repeatedly reflected within the room.

Materials such as curtains, carpets, upholstered seats, acoustic panels and suitable wall coverings absorb part of the incident sound energy rather than reflecting all of it.

Useful applications of multiple reflection

Megaphones and horns

Megaphones, loudhailers and horn-shaped instruments guide sound mainly in a preferred direction. Their shapes help direct sound towards an audience rather than allowing it to spread equally in all directions.

Stethoscopes

A stethoscope allows a doctor to listen to internal body sounds, particularly those of the heart and lungs.

In the school-level explanation, sound reaches the listener through the instrument's tubing with the help of multiple reflections and transmission through the enclosed path.

Curved ceilings and soundboards

Concert halls and auditoriums may use suitably shaped ceilings and sound-reflecting surfaces to direct sound towards different parts of the audience.

A soundboard placed behind a speaker or performer can reflect sound towards listeners.

Therefore, reflection is not always undesirable. Its usefulness depends on how the reflected sound reaches the listener.

For clear speech, unnecessary prolonged reflections should be reduced. For effective sound distribution, suitably directed reflections can be useful.

Prelims focus

  • Echo is a separately heard reflected sound.
  • Reverberation is the persistence of sound due to repeated reflections.
  • Excessive reverberation reduces speech clarity.
  • Sound-absorbing materials help control reverberation.
  • Megaphones, soundboards and suitably shaped hall ceilings use sound reflection beneficially.
  • Trap: Reverberation does not require each reflected sound to be separately heard.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 12, Sound, sections 12.3.2–12.3.3, printed pages 168–169; GCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 11, Sound, sections 11.3.2–11.3.3.]

pictures.alt: Two hall diagrams compare overlapping reflections that blur speech with absorbing surfaces that reduce lingering sound while retaining useful reflections.
pictures.caption: Sound-absorbing surfaces reduce repeated reflections and improve speech clarity.

title: Reverberation and Applications of Multiple Reflection

body:
How the human ear detects sound

Hearing begins when sound waves reach the ear. The ear detects pressure variations and converts them into signals that the brain interprets as sound.

The outer ear, called the pinna, collects sound waves and directs them into the auditory canal.

At the end of the auditory canal is a thin membrane called the eardrum, or tympanic membrane. Sound pressure variations cause this membrane to vibrate.

Three small bones in the middle ear transmit the vibrations towards the inner ear. In the inner ear, the cochlea converts the mechanical vibrations into electrical signals. These signals travel through the auditory nerve to the brain.

Normal audible range of humans

The approximate audible frequency range of a healthy young human ear extends from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.

This upper value is also written as 20 kHz, because 1 kHz equals 1000 Hz.

The range is approximate, not an identical fixed limit for every person. Hearing sensitivity varies among individuals and often decreases at higher frequencies with increasing age.

Classification of sound by frequency

Infrasonic sound

Sound with a frequency below 20 Hz is called infrasonic sound or infrasound.

Its vibrations are generally too slow to be detected as ordinary sound by the human ear.

Some animals, including elephants and certain whales, produce low-frequency sounds that can extend into the infrasonic range.

Audible sound

Sound within approximately 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz is in the normal human audible range.

Ordinary speech and many musical sounds contain frequencies within this range.

Ultrasonic sound

Sound with a frequency above 20,000 Hz is called ultrasonic sound or ultrasound.

Ultrasound lies above the normal upper limit of human hearing.

Some animals, such as bats and dolphins, produce and detect ultrasonic sounds.

Do all animals have the same hearing range?

No. Different animals have different hearing abilities.

Dogs can hear some frequencies higher than the normal upper limit of human hearing. Certain dog whistles use high-frequency sounds that may be difficult or impossible for humans to hear.

Bats use high-frequency sounds to detect objects and locate prey. Dolphins also use sound for underwater navigation and detection.

Elephants can use very low-frequency sounds for communication.

These examples demonstrate that the human audible range is not the universal hearing range of all animals.

Inaudible does not mean nonexistent

A sound outside the normal human hearing range is still a sound wave. If a suitable material medium is present, it can propagate even when humans cannot hear it.

Similarly, being within the audible frequency range does not guarantee that a sound will be heard. A sound may be too weak for the listener to detect.

Frequency and loudness are separate conditions. A sound may have an audible frequency but insufficient intensity to be heard. A very strong ultrasonic wave remains outside the normal human hearing range because its frequency is too high.

Prelims focus

  • The approximate human audible range is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
  • Infrasound has a frequency below 20 Hz.
  • Ultrasound has a frequency above 20,000 Hz.
  • The eardrum vibrates in response to sound waves.
  • The cochlea converts mechanical vibrations into electrical signals.
  • Bats and dolphins use high-frequency sounds for detection and navigation.
  • Trap: Ultrasound is not sound that cannot travel; it is sound above the normal human audible frequency range.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 12, Sound, sections 12.4 and 12.6, printed pages 169–172; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 13, Sound, sections 13.4–13.6; GCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 11, Sound, section 11.4.]

pictures.alt: Sound passes through the pinna, canal, eardrum and middle-ear bones; the cochlea converts vibrations into electrical signals carried to the brain.
pictures.caption: The ear converts sound vibrations into signals interpreted by the brain.

pictures.alt: Frequency rises from infrasound below 20 Hz, through normal human hearing at approximately 20–20,000 Hz, to ultrasound above 20,000 Hz.
pictures.caption: Sound is classified as infrasonic, audible or ultrasonic according to frequency.

title: Human Hearing and the Audible Frequency Range

body:
What makes ultrasound useful?

Ultrasound consists of sound waves with frequencies above 20,000 Hz, or 20 kHz.

Although ultrasound is normally inaudible to humans, it remains a mechanical wave and therefore requires a material medium for propagation.

Ultrasound obeys the general principles of sound propagation and reflection. Its relatively high frequency gives it a comparatively short wavelength in a particular medium.

Shorter wavelengths can help ultrasound interact with relatively small structures, making it useful in imaging and defect detection.

Medical imaging with ultrasound

Ultrasound is widely used to examine internal structures of the human body.

In ultrasonography, an ultrasound probe sends high-frequency sound waves into the body. When these waves encounter boundaries between tissues with different acoustic properties, part of the sound is reflected.

The returning echoes are detected and processed to form images of internal structures.

Ultrasonography can be used to examine organs such as the liver, kidneys, gall bladder and uterus.

It is also used during pregnancy to examine the developing foetus.

Echocardiography

Echocardiography is the application of ultrasound imaging to examine the heart.

Ultrasound reflections from cardiac structures are processed to obtain images of the heart and assess aspects of its movement and function.

Thus, echocardiography is a specific medical application of the broader principle of ultrasonography.

Detecting cracks in metal objects

Ultrasound can be used to detect internal cracks or defects in metal objects without cutting them open.

When ultrasonic waves enter a metal block, a hidden crack may reflect part of the sound energy. Detecting and analysing these reflected waves can reveal the presence of the defect.

This technique is useful because internal cracks may not be visible from the outside.

Ultrasonic cleaning

Ultrasonic cleaning uses high-frequency vibrations transmitted through a suitable cleaning liquid.

These vibrations help remove dirt, grease and other unwanted particles from surfaces, including areas that are difficult to clean by ordinary methods.

It is particularly useful for objects with small openings, grooves or complicated shapes.

Other medical applications

Specialised medical procedures can use focused acoustic energy to fragment certain urinary stones into smaller pieces. This is a therapeutic use of acoustic waves rather than ordinary diagnostic ultrasound imaging.

Diagnostic ultrasound is also different from X-ray imaging. Ultrasound uses mechanical sound waves, whereas X-rays are electromagnetic radiation.

The common principle behind these applications

The same basic physics supports several different uses:

  • Medical imaging: Reflected ultrasound provides information about internal tissue boundaries.
  • Metal inspection: Reflections help locate hidden discontinuities or defects.
  • Ultrasonic cleaning: High-frequency acoustic energy in a liquid assists the removal of contamination.

In the first 2 applications, reflected waves provide information about structures. In cleaning, acoustic energy is used mainly to assist a physical process.

Prelims focus

  • Ultrasound has a frequency above 20 kHz.
  • Ultrasound is a mechanical wave and needs a material medium.
  • Ultrasonography produces images using reflected ultrasound.
  • Echocardiography is ultrasound examination of the heart.
  • Ultrasound can help detect hidden cracks in metal objects.
  • Ultrasonic cleaning uses high-frequency acoustic energy in a liquid.
  • Trap: Ultrasound is not an electromagnetic wave like an X-ray.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 12, Sound, sections 12.4–12.5, printed pages 170–171; GCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 11, Sound, section 11.5, Applications of Ultrasound.]

pictures.alt: Medical imaging and metal inspection detect reflected ultrasound; ultrasonic cleaning uses vibrations in liquid to dislodge dirt.
pictures.caption: Ultrasound can provide medical images, reveal hidden cracks and assist cleaning.

title: Ultrasound and Its Important Applications
